In the Irish traditional music revival of the 1960s it drew attention through the composer Seán Ó Riada and through its use by traditional bands. It also appears in Scotland, Cape Breton, Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island and Galicia, often in line-ups with bagpipes and fiddles.

One hand sits inside the drum, and the area and pressure of that hand change the tension of the head, and with it the pitch and the timbre; the other hand strikes with the bare hand or a wooden tipper, and a brush-ended tipper or a stroke on the rim can be used for contrast. Modern tuning systems let the head be adjusted to the weather. Beside a tambourine with jingles, or the English sieve drum, the version without jingles depends more on the vibration of the head and on the pressure of the hand inside, and its colour can shift from rhythmic to following the phrasing of a melody.
愛爾蘭手鼓為框鼓，鼓框以木材製成，來源提及柳枝可作框；鼓面以山羊皮釘於一側，亦有: The bodhrán is a frame drum: the frame is made of wood, and the source mentions willow for it; the head is goatskin tacked onto one side, though synthetic or other animal skins are also used, and the other side is open. Early household versions used a willow frame, a leather head and pennies as jingles. One or two crossbars may run inside the frame, and some modern professional models have a mechanical tuning system, with the tension of the head set by a hex key. The tipper was once made from a double-headed knuckle bone; today it is usually ash, holly or hickory, and brush-ended tippers also exist. The other materials are not recorded.

Its name first appears in manuscripts of the fifteenth to the early seventeenth centuries. In the early twentieth century it was mostly a frame drum made at home on farms, and by 1946 there is film of one with jingles played with a tipper. In the Irish traditional music revival of the 1960s, promoted by Seán Ó Riada and others, it became a legitimate instrument; it appeared at an Irish festival only in 1973. It then spread with recordings through the Celtic music world, to Scotland, Newfoundland and elsewhere.

The bodhrán is a Celtic frame drum, a membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 211.311. The frame is about 25 to 65 cm in diameter, commonly 35 to 45 cm, and 9 to 20 cm deep; a goatskin is usually tacked to one side and the other side is open, and the player keeps one hand against the inside of the skin to control pitch and timbre. You play sitting down, with the drum held upright on the thigh, striking with the bare hand or a wooden tipper. It is used in Irish traditional music, and also appears in the Celtic music world, in Scotland, Cape Breton and elsewhere, commonly in band accompaniment and at traditional music occasions.
演奏者多坐姿，將鼓垂直置於大腿，以上身與左臂支撐；右手持雙頭或單頭敲棒（或徒手）: Players usually sit, resting the drum upright on the thigh and supporting it with the body and the left arm; the right hand strikes the head with a double-ended or single-ended tipper (or the bare hand), while the left hand reaches inside and presses the skin, changing its tension, pitch and timbre. A beginner can first practise holding the drum steadily and striking it, then use a double-ended tipper in the Kerry style and a single-ended one in the Limerick style, and may strike the rim for contrast.
